niche: Obscure business autopsies, counter-intuitive money math, and weird economic mechanics: bizarre corporate collapses, unglamorous micro-monopolies, perverse incentives (Cobra Effects), contract loopholes, and freak supply-chain dominos backed by hard numbers (pre-2015 cases preferred; real archival photos, SEC filings, headlines, and company records; no mainstream clichés, no financial advice)
audience: Curious viewers aged 18 to 45 in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia interested in finance, bizarre business trivia, economics, game theory, and how money really works behind the scenes, watching Shorts while scrolling
tone: Like a sharp forensic accountant explaining a wild scandal over drinks: opens inside a shocking dollar figure or fatal paradox, moves fast with tight cause-and-effect beats (so / but / you see), exposes the exact math or incentive loophole, and ends on a seamless grammatical bridge that loops back to the start
done_topics: In 1923, after Wall Street short sellers tried to tank his grocery chain Piggly Wiggly, founder Clarence Saunders borrowed $10 million and quietly bought up 198,872 of the company's 200,000 existing shares—cornering 99.4% of the stock and trapping Wall Street for millions until the New York Stock Exchange changed its own rules mid-trade to save its members and bankrupt him.
